item.title: Two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs is NP-hard
item.description: arXiv:2610.31719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a fixed straight-line drawing of a complete graph, we seek a two-colouring of its edges that minimizes the number of monochromatic crossing pairs. We prove that the threshold decision problem is NP-complete, even when the vertices are in general position and have integer coordinates of polynomial binary length. Thus exact minimization is NP-hard, answering the complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019. The reduction is from MaxCut on permutation graphs. Its main difficulty is to control the edges required by completeness, whose colours must remain free. We construct a large comparison grid with two stable colour phases and use additional points to assign costs to the edges that encode the source graph. A geometric separation eliminates one large class of unwanted crossings. The costs of all remaining edges are included in a computable baseline and bounded errors, with each unit of the source objective amplified beyond the total error. The construction is deterministic and has polynomial size and coordinate bit length.
item.dc:creator: Zhe Zhang

item.title: Deterministic Constructions of Reed-Solomon Codes Beyond the Johnson Bound
item.description: arXiv:2610.31922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a deterministic quasipolynomial-time construction of Reed-Solomon codes that are list-decodable beyond the Johnson radius. Specifically, for every $\epsilon\in(0,1]$ and all sufficiently large $n$, we construct an $[n,k]$ Reed-Solomon code of rate $R=\Omega(\epsilon/(1+\log(1/\epsilon)))$ over a field of size $(nk)^{quasi-poly(nk)}$ that is $(1-\epsilon,O(1/\epsilon))$ list-decodable. The construction runs in quasi-poly(nk) time. We also give a deterministic construction of $[n,k]$-MDS$(3)$ Reed-Solomon codes for all integers $1\leq k<n$, with the same asymptotic bounds on field size and construction time. In the constant-rate regime, our field-size bound substantially improves the bound of $O(n^{k^{2k}})$ achieved by Roth's construction (Roth, IEEE TIT 2022). Our constructions exploit a connection to polynomial identity testing for read-once determinants, together with the quasipolynomial isolating-weight construction of Gurjar and Thierauf for linear matroid intersection (Gurjar and Thierauf, STOC 2017 and Computational Complexity 2020).
item.dc:creator: Abhranil Chatterjee, Sumanta Ghosh, Zeyu Guo, Rohit Gurjar, Roshan Raj

item.title: On the Propeller Conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2610.32158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We simplify and improve OpenAI's proof of the propeller conjecture of Khot and Naor from 2008: the sum of the squared lengths of the Gaussian moments of any partition of Euclidean space is at most $9/(8\pi)$. We show equality only occurs for three 120 degree sectors in the plane (up to symmetries, measure zero changes, and taking orthogonal cross products with Euclidean space). We also remove computer assistance from the three-dimensional case of the conjecture, which previously used an epsilon net traversal.
item.dc:creator: Steven Heilman

item.title: Settling Nondeterministic Communication Complexity of Graph Connectivity
item.description: arXiv:2610.32346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining the communication complexity of graph connectivity has been one of the longest standing open problems in communication complexity since the seminal work of Babai, Frankl, and Simon [FOCS'86]. A simple protocol transmits a spanning forest using $O(N\log N)$ communication on $N$-vertex graphs. While this was shown optimal for deterministic protocols by Hajnal, Maass, and Tur\'an [STOC'88], the optimal nondeterministic and randomized complexities have remained unresolved for decades. We settle the nondeterministic communication complexity of graph connectivity by proving an optimal $\Omega(N\log N)$ lower bound. The best prior bound was $\Omega(N\log\log N)$ due to Raz and Spieker [Combinatorica'95]. Our bound is shown by upper bounding the maximum size of $1$-monochromatic rectangles. Generalizing our techniques to weighted, almost $1$-monochromatic rectangles yields an $\Omega(N \cdot \log(\min(1/\varepsilon,N)))$ lower bound for randomized protocols with error probability $\varepsilon$. In particular, this bound is optimal for any polynomially small $\varepsilon$. For constant error probability, we also prove that any $r$-round protocol requires $\Omega(N/r \cdot \log N)$ communication, which is optimal for every constant $r$. Previously, optimal $\Omega(N\log N)$ lower bounds for graph connectivity were known only for $1$-round [Sun, Woodruff; APPROX/RANDOM'15] and $2$-round protocols [Radhakrishnan, Reddy, Venkat; ITCS'26]. Our proof introduces a new communication problem which can be viewed as a composition of inner product and pointer chasing problems. Our lower bounds can be extended to other fundamental graph properties, and also imply optimality of known query and streaming algorithms for related problems.
item.dc:creator: Zhijun Zhang

item.title: Stable Set Reconfiguration in Dense Digraphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.32402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In a directed graph, a stable (or acyclic) set is a set which does not induce a directed cycle. Given a directed graph and two acyclic sets of the same size, the Acyclic-Set-Reconfiguration with Directed Token Sliding (ASR) problem asks whether one can, by iteratively replacing a vertex by an adjacent one, transform the first set into the second one, while maintaining acyclicity during the transformation. In this work, we present a study of the complexity of ASR and provide an FPT algorithm for semi-complete digraphs, when parametrized by the size of the sets being reconfigured, the directed pathwidth (or equivalently, the directed treewidth) of the instance, and a newly introduced parameter called the iteration of the reconfiguration sequence. To the best of our knowledge, the reconfiguration of stable sets has only been studied on undirected graphs, or (more recently) on sparse directed graphs.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Houdaigoui, Nacim Oijid, Matthieu Petiteau, Alexandre Vigny

item.title: Deterministic Root-Finding over Finite Fields with Elliptic Curves
item.description: arXiv:2610.32508v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Finding the roots of a polynomial over a finite field $\mathbb F_q$ in deterministic polynomial time is a long-standing open problem. Classical deterministic methods work in the multiplicative group $\mathbb F_q^\times$ and are efficient only when $q-1$ is smooth, which is rarely the case. We propose a method that replaces $\mathbb F_q^\times$ by the groups of rational points of an elliptic curve $E$ and of its quadratic twist $\widetilde E$. The computation splits into an offline phase, which depends only on $\mathbb F_q$ and outputs a short \emph{elliptic preprocessing datum} $\mathcal D$, and an online phase, which processes the input polynomial. Writing $\Xi(\mathcal D)$ for the largest prime factor of $\lvert E(\mathbb F_q)\rvert\cdot\lvert\widetilde E(\mathbb F_q)\rvert$, the online phase is deterministic and finds the roots of any $f\in\mathbb F_q[X]$ of degree $n$ within $\widetilde O(\Xi(\mathcal D)^2\,n\log^2 q+n^\omega\log q+n\log^3 q)$ operations in $\mathbb F_q$. A precursor of our method is an algorithm by R\'onyai, which recovers the roots through Galois computations over number fields, relies on GRH, and comes with a polynomial bound of unspecified degree; in contrast, our online phase works entirely over $\mathbb F_q$ and is unconditional. Moreover, $\mathcal D$ can be certified deterministically and unconditionally in time polynomial in $\log q$ and $\Xi(\mathcal D)$. We conjecture that every $\mathbb F_q$ of large enough characteristic admits a datum with $\Xi(\mathcal D)\leq(\log q)^{O(1)}$, and support this with a heuristic and with experiments. Constructing such a datum in polynomial time remains open.
item.dc:creator: Pierre-Jean Spaenlehauer

item.title: On the complexity of Medvedev reducibility
item.description: arXiv:2610.32522v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Medvedev lattice is a tool used to classify the complexity of effective closed sets. In this article, we are interested in the complexity of using this tool. In particular, we study the complexity of deciding whether two effective closed sets have the same degree, when one is fixed and the other is given as input. This problem is naturally~$\Sigma^0_3$, and among other results, we show that for all degrees except the maximal one, the problem reaches its maximal complexity. It turns out that the argument is not uniform and depends on the self-similarity of the fixed degree, a notion that we introduce in this article. The complexity of having maximal degree is particularly difficult to establish, but we obtain a lower bound that almost matches the upper bound. We also show that deciding whether an effective closed set has a degree incomparable with a fixed degree $d$ is $\Pi^0_3$-complete whenever $\mathbf{0}_s <_s d <_s \mathbf{1}_s$.
item.dc:creator: Remi Pallen

item.title: Structure and Exact Certification of Nonnegative Tensor Decompositions
item.description: arXiv:2610.32787v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the structure and exact certification of nonnegative tensor decompositions supplied through rational factor matrices. Every failure of minimality or essential uniqueness contains an irreducible positive exchange between $p$ supplied terms and $q$ competing terms. A dimension count based on the Lovitz--Petrov splitting theorem bounds the effective order of such an exchange, the sum over the modes of the joint factor-span dimension minus one, by $p+q-2$, and this bound is attained at every supplied length $R\ge2$. After eliminating ambient-row variables by the Farkas lemma, the resulting semialgebraic systems have fewer than $2R^2$ real variables. For input bit length $L$, this gives a deterministic $G(R)L^{O(R^2)}$-time algorithm that computes the nonnegative rank and an exact minimum-length decomposition, decides minimality and essential uniqueness, and returns exact witnesses when either property fails. The exponent is independent of the tensor order and the mode dimensions. For Lebesgue moment tensors, positive quadrature determines the nonnegative rank and the uniqueness behavior, and some rational length-$R$ inputs force a common field of degree at least $\lfloor R/2\rfloor!$ for any exact minimum-length output. As an illustration, an implementation resolves all 114 instances left inconclusive by earlier positive-scattering criteria, of which 95 are minimal and essentially unique and 19 are minimal but nonunique.
item.dc:creator: Haoming Wang, Ming Yuan

item.title: On the Complexity of Bilevel Linear and Quadratic Programs in Fixed Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2511.15592v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the computational complexity of bilevel linear programs (BLPs) and bilevel quadratic programs (BQPs) with continuous variables under restrictions on the numbers of variables or constraints. Our results identify new transitions between computational complexity regimes that are inherent to the hierarchical structure of bilevel optimization problems and have no direct counterparts in single-level optimization. First, we demonstrate that, under comparable assumptions, the pessimistic formulation can be computationally harder than its optimistic counterpart. Specifically, while optimistic BLPs are known to be polynomially solvable when the number of follower variables is fixed, we prove that the corresponding pessimistic problem is strongly NP-complete. We also show that this complexity transition is tied to the presence of a nonfixed number of coupling constraints. Second, we show that, in the pessimistic setting with a fixed number of follower constraints, BLPs are polynomially solvable, whereas replacing the follower's linear objective function with a convex quadratic one renders the problem NP-hard. Importantly, this complexity transition occurs even in the absence of coupling constraints. Finally, we demonstrate that replacing a convex quadratic follower objective with a nonconvex quadratic one renders the optimistic problem NP-hard, even when both follower dimensions are fixed and small.
item.dc:creator: Sergey S. Ketkov, Oleg A. Prokopyev

item.title: On the complexity of Multipacking
item.description: arXiv:2602.07982v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A \emph{multipacking} in an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ is a set $M\subseteq V$ such that for every vertex $v\in V$ and for every integer $r\geq 1$, the ball of radius $r$ around $v$ contains at most $r$ vertices of $M$, that is, there are at most $r$ vertices in $M$ at a distance at most $r$ from $v$ in $G$. The \textsc{Multipacking} problem asks whether a graph contains a multipacking of size at least $k$. For more than a decade, it remained an open question whether the \textsc{Multipacking} problem is \textsc{NP}-complete or solvable in polynomial time. Whereas the problem is known to be polynomial-time solvable for certain graph classes (e.g., strongly chordal graphs, grids, etc). Foucaud, Gras, Perez, and Sikora [\textit{Algorithmica} 2021] made a step towards solving the open question by showing that the \textsc{Multipacking} problem is \textsc{NP}-complete for directed graphs and it is \textsc{W[1]}-hard when parameterized by the solution size. We prove that the \textsc{Multipacking} problem is \textsc{NP}-complete and \textsc{W[2]}-hard on undirected graphs when parameterized by the solution size. These hardness results also hold for chordal, bipartite, claw-free, and chordal $\cap$ $\frac{1}{2}$-hyperbolic graphs. Chordal $\cap$ $\frac{1}{2}$-hyperbolic graph class contains strongly chordal graphs, where the problem is polynomial-time solvable. We further establish \textsc{NP}-completeness on regular and CONV graphs (intersection graphs of convex sets in the plane). On the positive side, we present an exact $O(1.53^n)$-time algorithm for general $n$-vertex graphs, breaking the $2^n$ barrier.
item.dc:creator: Sandip Das, Sk Samim Islam, Daniel Lokshtanov

item.title: A General Composition Theorem for Approximate Degree
item.description: arXiv:2609.30139v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A longstanding open question in Boolean function complexity asks whether approximate degree composes multiplicatively under block composition. Although a general multiplicative upper bound is known, matching lower bounds have previously been established only for restricted classes of functions. We resolve this question for all total Boolean functions by proving the matching lower bound. Together with Sherstov's upper bound, our result shows that, for every pair of total Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ and $g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}$, \[ \widetilde{deg}(f\circ g) = \Theta\!\left( \widetilde{deg}(f)\,\widetilde{deg}(g) \right), \] where $\widetilde{deg}$ denotes constant-error approximate degree. We also consider the analogous question for exact quantum query complexity and give a counterexample showing that multiplicative composition fails in this setting.
item.dc:creator: Samruddhi Pednekar, Supartha Podder

item.title: On the Hardness of $4$-to-$1$ Games with Perfect Completeness
item.description: arXiv:2610.12378v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that for all $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a positive integer $k$ such that given a $4$-to-$1$ game $\Psi$ with alphabet size at most $k$, it is $\mathbf{NP}$-hard to distinguish between the case that $\mathrm{val}(\Psi)=1$ and the case that $\mathrm{val}(\Psi)\leq \varepsilon$. This confirms the $4$-to-$1$ Games Conjecture from [Khot, \textit{CCC 2002}]. Previously, the best known result, due to [Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, Safra], established the almost-perfect completeness version (but applied to the stricter problem of $2$-to-$1$ games). Using results from the literature, we get the following implications: (1) for all $k\in \mathbb{N}$, given a $3$-colorable graph $G$, it is $\mathbf{NP}$-hard to find a proper $k$-coloring; (2) for all $\delta>0$, given a $2$-colorable $3$-uniform hypergraph $G$, it is $\mathbf{NP}$-hard to find in it an independent set containing at least $\delta$ fraction of the vertices. Our proof is a three-step construction that builds on the two-step framework of [Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, Safra]. In the outer-PCP step, we use quadratic equations to gain perfect completeness. We then construct a new middle PCP that performs low-rank tests while preserving a key covering property. Finally, we construct a new inner PCP based on a tensor of the standard Grassmann encoding with its low-rank variant due to [Golowich, FOCS 2023].
item.dc:creator: Yumou Fei, Dor Minzer, Shuo Wang

item.title: Adversarial Problems and the Limits of Uniform Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2512.08149v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A general method of resolution can take part in forming problems once their language represents the method itself. A fixed formation rule gives each sound resolver a presentation it cannot answer. Admitting the diagnosis yields a sound successor with an instance of its own. For standard arithmetical theories $\mathrm{T}$, the instance is $\mathsf{HA}$-provably equivalent to $\mathrm{Con}(\mathrm{T})$. A theory that decides its own instance asserts a false sentence. The $m$-th iterated independence question is equivalent to the instance $m$ stages later. No effective admission policy with consistent union closes the regress. A noncomputable answer function resolves all program indices, while a false assertion of resolution supplies no warrant. At feasible scale, bounded self-consistency is cheap. A clocked G\"odel sentence gives an unconditional gap relative to its short binary description, but no superpolynomial lower bound in the window size. The arithmetic identity motivates studying bounded consistency of the successor theory, as in a conjecture of Pudl\'ak. We state its finitely axiomatized case and prove that it implies $\mathcal{NP}\ne\mathrm{co}\mathcal{NP}$. The conjecture motivates a feasible analogue, but does not establish all clauses of the unbounded barrier.
item.dc:creator: Milan Rosko
